Clear the draw page: fill the 32 pages from $07 ($20 or $40) with $80, black.

Clip a shape to the screen's 40 byte columns: $15 keeps its width, $14 is the first column drawn, $16 the bytes cut off at the left, and $0E becomes the bytes drawn on each row. A negative column, the shape starting left of the screen, cuts it at the left edge, a shape that would run past column 39 is cut at the right, and one wholly off the screen is not drawn ($1A2F). Then the mode ($0F) is written into the instruction at $19E6: ORA ($00),Y for 0, AND ($00),Y for a negative mode, two NOPs for a positive one, so that the STA after it ORs, masks or stores.
The same LDA $0F twice.

Draw the rows: for each of the $0D rows, the row's address on the draw page from the row tables ($0800, $08C0 plus $07) and $14. When bytes were cut at the left, the last one cut is read only for the dots it carries into the first byte drawn. The first byte keeps the screen's dots to the left of the shape ($1A34), each byte is the shape's dots shifted by $10 ($1A84) with the dots carried from the byte before, and the dots carried out of the last byte go into the next screen byte ($19F8) unless it is past column 39.
The instruction the mode writes: ORA ($00),Y, AND ($00),Y, or two NOPs, before the STA ($00),Y that follows.
The second byte of the instruction at $19E6: $00 for ORA and AND ($00),Y, or a NOP in store mode.

The dots carried past the shape's last byte: ORed onto the screen in mode 0; in store mode the screen keeps its own dots to the right of them ($1A3B); in AND mode the mask's carried dots are set to the right ($1A3B) and ANDed.
Done: X and Y back from $18 and $17.
For a dot offset of 0-6, the screen's dots kept to the left of a shape's first dot, with bit 7 set: none, then one to six.
For a dot offset of 0-6, the screen's dots kept to the right of the dots carried out of a shape's last byte.
Draw a shape: read its header ($1A61), clip it and draw it ($1927), and put the pointer back ($1AEB).
Draw a shape with its right edge at column $05: the column less the width, plus one, for the drawing, then $05 back.
Read a shape's header: keep its pointer in $1B/$1C, X in $18 and Y in $17, its height in rows in $0D and its width in bytes in $0E, and move ($03) on to the first row.

Shift the seven dots of the shape byte in A right by $10 dots (0-6): returns the dots that stay in this byte, moved along, and puts in $1A the dots pushed out into the next byte. A dot moves right on the screen as it moves up a bit, since bit 0 is the leftmost dot.
Put the shape pointer back from $1B/$1C.

Draw a shape mirrored. The dot offset becomes 7 less $10 (or, at 0, the column one less), so that the mirrored shape ends where the shape would have started. The shape is clipped as $1927 does, $1D saying which side was cut (1 the left, $FF the right), and each row is read from its last byte back to its first, every byte through the reversal table at $0980 (read as $0900 + X with bit 7 set) so that its dots come out in reverse order. The mode works as for $1903, through the instruction at $1BF2. $05 and $10 come back at the end ($1C50).

The demo hero's brain, which plays the hero in the demo in place of the player ($B6E2) and ends in the command routine ($6540). With the guard lying dead (legs $13 at $70): forward ($29 = 1), standing up first ($9B) from the stance. Standing ($2F): forward until the guard ($72) is less than $4A columns ahead, then the stance. In the stance with no guard alive ($5E), or 12 columns or more from him ($33): nothing. Nearer, a random height ($A0AF); a random number at or above $DB does nothing; otherwise another, against four thresholds read as base + X with X the distance held to 7-11: at or above the first ($A08E-$A092) nothing, the second ($A093-$A097) a kick ($C5), the third ($A098-$A09C) a punch ($D7), the fourth ($A09D-$A0A1) a step forward, and below it a step back. The steps are the stick's movement ($29 = 1 or $FF, A the same, which the command routine takes as no command) and are taken only in the stance's pose (legs 6).

Forward ($29 = 1) and the movement alone. The four threshold tables have their bases at $A087, $A08C, $A091 and $A096 and are read as base + X with X = 7-11, so the bytes read start after this code, at $A08E.

Move the scene with the hero, once a frame. On the first screen ($44 = 0) a hero at column $2A or more sets $AF when no guard is coming on ($30), which in the title ends the demo ($B5D3); with a guard coming on, a hero at column $21 or more would take the scene to the second screen ($B2EC), but nothing in the title sets $30, so the demo stays on the first screen. On the second screen, at column $2A or more, $D0 = 2. A hero left of column 3 goes back to the first screen ($B2CF) from the second, and on the first starts the scene scrolling right. Elsewhere the scene scrolls to bring him to column $0F: from the left of it towards the right ($B381), from the right of it towards the left ($B30F). The scroll ($52) runs from $30 down to $1B on the first screen, and from $0B down on the second.

Scroll towards the left: the speed $53 is brought two dots a frame towards -4 (in the stance), -6 (standing) or -10 (running, legs sequence $42-$49).
